<reason>PRO built a coherent causal story (volatility, Dutch disease, intergenerational conversion, political entitlement dynamics) and, crucially, established early via Alaska that distribution can sit downstream of a fund while the reverse is impossible—CON never squarely neutralized this. PRO's pressure questions were the decisive instrument: Q1 forced CON to admit the dividend "falls to zero" in a sustained bust, and Q2 extracted the concession that the steadily supported child is better protected. PRO's closing then crystallized these admissions memorably ("asking every household in a poor country to run its own sovereign wealth fund, alone, without diversification"). CON argued competently and honestly—the debt-repayment durability point and the sufficiency objection remained genuinely live—and its capture critique was reasonable, but it never offered a comparative reason why those gains outweigh pooled risk-smoothing, and its own design concessions (pacing, treasury holding, temporary payments) kept collapsing toward PRO's instrument. PRO's clipped Rebuttal 2 is a small execution cost but did not remove the A1/A2 answers or the core weighing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Pressure Q1 ([A3.1]) asking what happens when copper stays low for three years, followed by CON's A1 admission that the dividend falls "potentially to zero" [B4.1], which PRO then converted in its closing into the frame that CON hands citizens the boom and then the bust while a fund is still paying.</best_rebuttal>
